strategy.headline: San Antonio wears silver and black every day, and Fiesta color on the days that count.
strategy.thesis: San Antonio is a one-team city, and silver and black is its civic dress. West Side abuelas wear it, and so do East Side families who remember the Iceman, Joint Base San Antonio households and Laredo road-trippers. Fans guard the Duncan-Popovich habit of restraint. Color lives elsewhere: Fiesta's pink, turquoise and marigold, the medal pins, conjunto and the West Side's sign-painted shopfronts. So does an East Side lineage that runs from George Gervin to the arena's own neighborhood. Keep core product monochrome and precise. Spend color only on occasions the city already keeps: the returning Fiesta-stripe City Edition, an April Fiesta drop, Cup Fridays and the Rodeo Road Trip. Make every cultural piece with credited, paid local artists from each side of town. The money is in price tiers for a price-aware, bilingual region that shops for whole families, led by an always-on Wembanyama youth ladder.

archetype.name: The Civic Family Contender
archetype.description: A multigenerational, Latino-majority, military-heavy fan base that spans the West, East and South Sides. It treats the Spurs as the city's shared family table and prizes humility over flash. After losing the 2026 Finals, it now expects a title.

pulse.teamMoment: The Spurs won the West in 2026 at 62-20, beating OKC 4-3 in the West finals, then lost the Finals 4-1 to the Knicks. They extended Wembanyama (5 years, $252M) and Fox through 2029-30. The core runs it back under Mitch Johnson, and they're title co-favorites with OKC. Opening night, Oct 20, is the West finals rematch with OKC. The Knicks come back on Christmas Day at MSG and on Mar 7 in San Antonio.
pulse.sentiment: Confident and hungry, not celebratory. Fans are proud of the West title, stung by the Knicks and protective of Spurs humility. They watch Project Marvel and the Frost Bank Center lease talks with civic interest, not alarm.

topInsights.title: Fiesta is the city's design system, and it lands on the first round
topInsights.insight: Fiesta's ten days in the second half of April overlap the first playoff round: Battle of Flowers, Fiesta Flambeau, NIOSA at La Villita. Thanks to its medal culture, locals already treat a hat or sash as a surface for collectible pins. Fans embraced the Fiesta-stripe City Edition because it turns that palette into stripes on black instead of costume.
topInsights.implication: Make April the market's biggest product moment. Pre-announce one Fiesta capsule and a four-medal set built to be worn at Fiesta events. Make them with local medal makers, and clear them with every Fiesta organization whose name or medal design appears.

topInsights.title: Restraint is the brand; color is the occasion
topInsights.insight: Thirty years of silver, black and white under Duncan and Popovich made understatement a civic value. Spurs gear gets worn every month, not just on game nights. The warmest nostalgia belongs to the teal, orange and fuchsia Fiesta era of 1989-2002, but fans want it as an accent on black, not a takeover.
topInsights.implication: Keep core product tonal and monochrome, with small, precise local details like woven labels and bilingual hang tags. Save loud color for City Edition, Fiesta and capsule drops.

topInsights.title: The hand-made West Side has never led a Spurs uniform
topInsights.insight: San Antonio's own craft is conjunto, the button accordion and bajo sexto that the Guadalupe's Tejano Conjunto Festival has championed for four decades. It's also Fiesta medals, made by hundreds of local organizations, and the hand-painted letters on West Side taquerias, panaderias and tire shops. Heritage nights have nodded to it. None of it has led a Spurs City Edition the way the Fiesta stripe has.
topInsights.implication: Commission named local letterers, printmakers and conjunto musicians for credited graphics now. Pitch a West Side City Edition concept for 2027-28, but only after Nike and the NBA confirm the design lock date.

topInsights.title: The East Side is the arena's neighborhood and the franchise's root
topInsights.insight: Frost Bank Center sits on the East Side, the historic heart of Black San Antonio. The fan lineage starts with George Gervin's Iceman finger-roll at HemisFair Arena and runs through David Robinson, Sean Elliott and Avery Johnson. Each January the city's MLK March, one of the largest in the country, walks through the same neighborhood. Project Marvel's planned downtown move makes the East Side's tie to the team a live question.
topInsights.implication: Add an East Side thread with its own credited Black San Antonio designers and institutions. Start with a Gervin-era heritage capsule (with Gervin's agreement) and a Black History Month and MLK week moment. Put the community first, and never let it read as a farewell to the neighborhood.

topInsights.title: Taste is set on the West Side; volume runs through malls and Academy
topInsights.insight: Cultural credibility comes from the West Side, Market Square and the Southtown and Blue Star scene. Volume flows through North Star, La Cantera, Ingram Park and South Park mall chains, Academy, Dick's and the Frost Bank Center team store. Independent sneaker culture is thinner than in Houston or Dallas.
topInsights.implication: Seed artist drops first in community pop-ups: the Guadalupe, First Fridays, Ingram Park. Then scale the stripe and core product at the volume doors through allocation and shop-in-shop quality. Don't build a flagship.

topInsights.title: Tier for the family of four, the E-5 and the Alamo Heights collector
topInsights.insight: This is a price-aware market. Spending clusters on the Texas August sales-tax holiday (items under $100), military 1st-and-15th paydays, Christmas and Las Posadas, and Fiesta. Flea markets like Traders Village set a bootleg price floor. And Wembanyama is now the role model for a generation of local kids.
topInsights.implication: Run the price ladder all year. Push a sub-$100 youth and tee tier for the holidays now, and peak it at the August tax holiday. Make the swingman the committed buy, and protect authentic and limited drops. Never chase flea-market prices with the top tier.

topInsights.title: Spurs Nation is a region, a border and now a global audience
topInsights.insight: The fan base runs to Laredo, Corpus Christi, the Rio Grande Valley and Monterrey. Mexican shoppers drive to La Cantera, North Star and the San Marcos outlets around Buen Fin and the December holidays. Ginobili's Latin American following and Wembanyama's French one, plus games in Austin, Paris and Manchester, make this a team that travels.
topInsights.implication: Make bilingual, Spanish-first copy the default on local drops, and time November promos to Buen Fin. Run an Austin game-week pop-up for the I-35 corridor. Give the international games a clean silver-and-black travel story.

scorecard.rationale: A title co-favorite led by Wembanyama, in a one-team region that runs to Mexico, puts fandom and opportunity near the top. Retail is ordinary mall-and-Academy volume, and the Fiesta and West Side culture is distinctive but narrower than the coastal giants' (brief scores: opportunity 82, culture 86, retail 56, fandom 90). Opportunity, culture and fandom run well above average. The Spurs are title co-favorites led by Wembanyama, in a one-team region that runs to Mexico. They have some of the league's most specific design material: Fiesta, conjunto, West Side craft and the East Side's Iceman lineage. Retail is ordinary: mall, Academy and arena-store volume in a price-aware market, with a thin independent sneaker scene and a real bootleg channel.

music.headline: The button accordion is San Antonio's instrument, and the Spurs live inside its music
music.summary: San Antonio music is a Mexican-American lineage: conjunto, orquesta Tejana, Chicano soul and Westside rock and R&B. It lives on in Tejano radio, dancehalls, Fiesta and a punk scene that mixes accordion with riot grrrl and garage. This is family-and-dancefloor music, and it shows up around the Spurs. Credit and partner with local musicians and poster artists instead of borrowing their look.

insights.title: Conjunto is the native sound
insights.detail: Conjunto grew up on the Westside: button accordion plus bajo sexto. The Tejano Conjunto Festival at the Guadalupe Cultural Arts Center has presented it every May for decades. Flaco Jimenez lived and worked here, won Grammys and made the accordion a global sound.
insights.implication: Treat the accordion, bajo sexto and dancehall as heritage cues. Build a Westside-rooted capsule around real players, with credit and payment. Skip the generic Mexican-American look.

insights.title: Tejano is the Spurs' family soundtrack
insights.detail: Tejano orquestas and conjuntos play quinceaneras, dancehalls, Fiesta stages and rodeo-season concerts across South Texas. The Spurs run Latin heritage nights that draw on that world, with bilingual Spanish-and-English game presentation. Selena was from Corpus Christi, but her legacy is Tejano's emotional center in San Antonio too.
insights.implication: Build around Tejano heritage nights and Selena-adjacent moments only with licensed or family-approved partners. Selena imagery is tightly controlled IP.

insights.title: Fiesta's posters and medals are a design tradition
insights.detail: April's Fiesta brings papel picado, collectible medals, royalty gowns, NIOSA and Battle of Flowers. Its poster and medal art is a long-running local design tradition. The Spurs' Fiesta-stripe City Edition already borrows the palette.
insights.implication: Extend the City Edition's colors into warm-ups, tees and headwear. Time any drop to April Fiesta and the playoff run. License the Fiesta Commission's marks.

insights.title: Westside rock and Chicano soul run rougher
insights.detail: Sunny Ozuna and Sunny & the Sunliners, the Sir Douglas Quintet and the Texas Tornados (Doug Sahm, Augie Meyers, Flaco Jimenez, Freddy Fender) fused R&B, garage rock, Tex-Mex and conjunto. Girl in a Coma and Piñata Protest carry the line into indie and punk.
insights.implication: This is the edgier counterpart to Tejano heritage. Mine it for graphics: 1960s garage-soul posters, record sleeves, lowrider-era script. Aim lifestyle product at younger, scene-literate fans.

insights.title: The military city keeps its own rhythm
insights.detail: San Antonio's four-base military community, Military City USA, lives alongside Tejano and country. Fort Sam, Lackland and Randolph families are a large part of the arena crowd. Country dancehalls like Floore's Country Store in Helotes sit next to the conjunto rooms.
insights.implication: Pair military-appreciation apparel with country and Tejano programming so it reads local. Don't reduce the market to one genre.

insights.title: The arena sounds bilingual, silver and black
insights.detail: Game presentation mixes English and Spanish. Local acts regularly play Frost Bank Center, the Alamodome and the Rodeo. With a Finals run behind them and Victor Wembanyama's French-international fan base, the building now draws more than Tejano.
insights.implication: Add a bilingual graphic layer, such as Spanish phrasing on tees. Keep a restrained silver-and-black base so the music-poster accents pop.

art.headline: Mission stone and sign-painted taquerías: a city whose look is made by hand
art.summary: San Antonio's look is hand-made and old: mission limestone, talavera tile, sign-painted taquerías and a 50-year Chicano poster and mural tradition rooted on the West Side. Each April, Fiesta adds the loudest palette and the city's most local object, the medal. The Fiesta-stripe City Edition proves the Spurs speak the language. Go past the stripe: commission San Antonio makers and credit them.

insights.title: Each April the whole city wears one palette
insights.detail: In April, the whole city dresses in one palette: papel picado strings, cascarones, flower crowns and the Fiesta medal. People collect the medals and pin them on hats and jackets. Trading them is a local ritual with its own pin-and-flair look.
insights.implication: Start from the Fiesta-stripe City Edition. Build a Fiesta-season capsule and a medal-style pin or patch system. Don't treat the palette as a one-off stripe.

insights.title: Chicano print and mural tradition is the credible spine
insights.detail: West Side institutions like Guadalupe Cultural Arts Center, and the Chicano screenprint and poster lineage (Cruz Ortiz and peers), give the city a hand-pulled, flat-color, high-contrast graphic voice. It reads as local, not decorative.
insights.implication: Brief artwork from San Antonio printmakers and muralists, and credit them on the product. Use screenprint and flat-color separations, not digital gradients.

insights.title: Limestone, tile and iron are the brand's architecture
insights.detail: Five Spanish missions (a UNESCO site), the Alamo facade, the Rose Window at Mission San Jose, talavera tile in Southtown and La Villita, and River Walk ironwork. Together they supply creamy limestone, cobalt-and-white tile geometry and arched silhouettes.
insights.implication: Use limestone cream and talavera blue as a quieter, premium palette beside the Fiesta brights, for tonal warm-up and travel pieces. Don't use the Alamo as a logo. It's a state-managed historic site and politically loaded.

insights.title: Spurs silver and black already fit
insights.detail: Silver and black reads as the city's year-round identity against Fiesta color. The Spurs have used Mexican-American heritage nights and Spanish-language Los Spurs branding for years.
insights.implication: Treat silver and black as the canvas and Fiesta color as the accent system, as the current City Edition does. Wembanyama's global audience means any local-art collab should also travel (Paris, Manchester games).

insights.title: Hand-painted signs set the typography
insights.detail: Taquerías, panaderías, botánicas, tire shops and West Side storefronts use hand-lettered sign-painter script, outlined block capitals and Spanish-English mixing. Tex-Mex bakery boxes and Mexican candy packaging add loud color blocking.
insights.implication: A hand-lettered wordmark from a local sign painter will out-read any digital script. Use it on graphic tees, warm-up tape and hangtags.

insights.title: The scene runs on festivals and months
insights.detail: Contemporary Art Month in March, Fiesta in April, Fotoseptiembre in the fall and Dia de los Muertos events around Nov 1-2. That makes four predictable windows when local art is in the public eye.
insights.implication: Time artist drops to Fiesta in April, when a deep playoff run is likely. Do the same for Dia de los Muertos in early November, during the NBA Cup group stage. Handle Muertos with community partners, and don't use skulls as decoration.

food.headline: Tex-Mex is a birthright here, served on flour tortillas and argued over at drive-ins
food.summary: San Antonio eats Mexican-American first, from a Tejano and Chicano lineage older than the skyline: the plaza Chili Queens, the Market Square panaderías, the West Side drive-ins. Breakfast tacos come on flour tortillas and barbacoa comes on Sunday. The places people defend are family-run and decades old. For the 2026 Finals runners-up, food is the shortest road from the court to the neighborhood table.

insights.title: The puffy taco could only be San Antonio
insights.detail: Fried-masa puffy tacos belong to the West Side drive-in tradition. Locals argue over Ray's Drive Inn and Henry's Puffy Tacos. Breakfast tacos on flour tortillas (bean and cheese, potato and egg, migas) are the daily ritual on every block.
insights.implication: A puffy-taco silhouette or a breakfast-taco foil-wrap graphic reads as insider in a way a generic taco icon never would. Keep it a small graphic or hangtag detail, not a costume.

insights.title: Mexican-American families built the table
insights.detail: Mi Tierra at Market Square, the panadería counters and the Christmas tamalada tradition come from Tejano and Mexican-American families who built the city's food economy. Spurs fandom in South Texas and across the border in Mexico overlaps heavily with this table.
insights.implication: Partner with San Antonio Latino chefs, bakers and illustrators, and credit them. Don't lift their imagery. Treat the community as the author of the cues, and pay it.

insights.title: H-E-B and Whataburger are civic brands you can wear
insights.detail: H-E-B is headquartered in San Antonio, and people wear its Texas-pride merchandise with sincerity. Whataburger, also headquartered here, has a fan-merch culture of its own, with its orange-and-white A-frame and stripes.
insights.implication: Both are third-party trademarks, so any reference needs a licensed collaboration. A co-branded capsule would carry local weight, but only through formal licensing.

insights.title: Fiesta feeds the city as the playoffs start
insights.detail: Fiesta runs through April with its medals, papel picado, cascarones, A Night in Old San Antonio and the Oyster Bake. All of it is food-driven. The Spurs' Fiesta-stripe City Edition already borrows the palette, and the playoffs run April to June.
insights.implication: Plan a Fiesta-week product and content drop for April. Let the City Edition story live in food and street color, not only on the court.

insights.title: Ice houses, not sports bars, are where neighborhoods gather
insights.detail: Open-air Texas ice houses like the Friendly Spot in Southtown play host to the beer, tacos and TV watch party. Food trucks park beside the picnic tables. Game nights spill into patios, taquerias and backyards.
insights.implication: Run watch parties at ice houses and taquerias with local food trucks. Design for patio weather: lightweight, sun-ready, easy to layer.

insights.title: The Pearl and Southtown carry the chef-driven layer
insights.detail: New chef-led spots cluster at the Pearl, anchored by the Culinary Institute of America campus and a Saturday farmers market, and in Southtown's restaurant and bar scene. Chefs like Steve McHugh and Johnny Hernandez are recognized voices.
insights.implication: Use the Pearl for premium and press-facing moments. Pair it with West Side and East Side family spots, so the story isn't all polish. Don't let the Pearl stand in for the whole city.

culture.headline: San Antonio wears its overlooked-Texas-city chip with pride
culture.summary: San Antonio carries a chip about being the overlooked Texas city: bigger than people assume, older than Houston or Dallas and proudly Mexican American. The Missions, Fiesta, conjunto and the state's largest military community feed that identity, and the Spurs tie it together. Fans treat the team's sober silver and black as a civic value. Come in through the city's own colors and signs, with local makers credited.

insights.title: Fiesta color works best as stripes
insights.detail: Fiesta San Antonio runs each April, with the Battle of Flowers Parade, Fiesta Flambeau and the River Parade. It's the city's biggest shared ritual, and its medal-pin culture, with hundreds of pins on a lanyard or hat, is a local status game. The 2025 Fiesta-stripe City Edition showed fans embrace the palette when it's abstracted into stripes.
insights.implication: Build Fiesta-derived color systems and pin or medal accessories. Time them to the pre-Fiesta window in March and April and to the playoff run. Skip literal skulls and sombreros.

insights.title: Pride in being Mexican American first, Texan second
insights.detail: Locals rep their Tejano and Chicano heritage on the West and South Sides, where conjunto accordion, bajo sexto, panaderias and lowrider culture are everyday, not nostalgia. Outsiders reduce the city to the River Walk and the Alamo. Locals find that thin.
insights.implication: Lead with neighborhood cues (Westside, Southside, 210) and partner with Chicano and Tejano artists and shops. Treat River Walk and Alamo iconography as the tourist layer.

insights.title: Spurs identity is restraint, and fans guard it
insights.detail: The Duncan, Ginobili, Parker and Popovich era made "team over star" a civic value. People who never go to games wear silver and black year-round. Fans now hold that legacy alongside Victor Wembanyama and the 2026 Finals run.
insights.implication: Keep core Spurs product clean and monochrome, with small, precise local details. Save the loud Fiesta color for City Edition and capsule drops.

insights.title: Military City USA is a real customer base
insights.detail: Joint Base San Antonio (Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, Randolph) makes the military and veteran community a large share of the metro. The Spurs hold a Military Appreciation night each season. Service families rotate in and out, and carry Spurs fandom worldwide.
insights.implication: Make a respectful service-heritage capsule for the Military Appreciation window, with camo-adjacent textures and branch-neutral language. Use veteran-owned partners, and no official insignia without licensing.

insights.title: Heat shapes the wardrobe
insights.detail: Summers are long and hot and winters mild, so people wear breathable fabrics, caps and guayabera-adjacent camp collars. The stock show and rodeo each February add boots and hats that locals wear without irony.
insights.implication: Lightweight mesh, cotton-linen blends, sun-protective hats and short-sleeve warm-ups sell most of the year. A western-yoke or snap-button detail has a real local basis.

insights.title: The 210 and the Alamo City nicknames travel on product
insights.detail: Locals use the 210 area code, "SA", "Alamo City" and "Spurs Nation" constantly. The Tower of the Americas silhouette is the skyline shorthand.
insights.implication: For tees and caps, the area code and the Tower of the Americas are the safest, most local marks, more so than the Alamo facade.

underground.headline: Fiesta taught the city to customize, and the underground never stopped
underground.summary: The city's strongest taste-setters come from Mexican American community life: lowrider and truck culture, Tejano and conjunto, and the Fiesta habit of covering yourself in pins, medals and flowers. Beneath them sit Southtown zines, DIY shows at the Paper Tiger, Bonham Exchange nightlife and Traders Village vintage. The Finals run and Wembanyama's anime and Pokemon fandom are pulling gaming and sneaker kids into a fan base that used to skew family and military. Remix the customization habits already here.

insights.title: Medals and pins came first
insights.detail: San Antonians wear Fiesta medals and pins in clusters on vests, sashes and hats. They already treat clothing as a collectible, tradeable surface, and the Fiesta-stripe City Edition plugs straight into that habit.
insights.implication: Build collectible add-ons for City Edition and Fiesta-week drops: enamel pins, swappable patches, medal-style jock tags. Fans can layer them the way they layer medals.

insights.title: Lowrider and truck culture owns paint, not logos
insights.detail: South and West Side car culture prizes candy and pearl paint, pinstriping, gold leaf and airbrushed murals. Chicano lowrider imagery ties to family and club identity, not brand names.
insights.implication: Translate it into gradient and fade colorways, pinstripe trim and metallic-foil detailing on Spurs product. Commission lowrider painters and pinstripers as credited collaborators, and don't copy their murals.

insights.title: Wembanyama pulled anime and gaming into the Spurs orbit
insights.detail: Wembanyama's openly nerdy tastes (anime and manga, Pokemon, fantasy novels) give gaming and anime fans a reason to wear Spurs gear that earlier eras never did. That includes the crowd that fills San Japan each summer.
insights.implication: Pursue Wembanyama-linked graphics and collectible-style drops through his Nike relationship, and test pop-ups at anime and gaming events. Any anime or Pokemon imagery needs third-party licensing.

insights.title: Queer nightlife has run for decades
insights.detail: The Bonham Exchange has anchored San Antonio's LGBTQ+ nightlife for decades, and drag and ballroom culture surrounds it. Pride in June is the annual peak.
insights.implication: Pay local drag and ballroom performers as partners and build a Pride-season capsule. Skip the one-night rainbow logo. Credit the creators and give proceeds to local organizations.

insights.title: Vintage and thrift runs through flea markets
insights.detail: Local resellers flip and remix vintage Spurs tees, 1999-era silver-and-black gear and Mexican soccer jerseys at Traders Village and the Mercado-area stalls.
insights.implication: Mine the Spurs archive (1990s-2000s graphics) for reissues. To earn credibility, partner with local resellers on a restocked-vintage or re-worked series.

insights.title: DIY music and art scenes are small and protective
insights.detail: Southtown, the Blue Star Arts Complex and mid-size DIY rooms like the Paper Tiger host zine, print and punk-adjacent gatherings. They distrust corporate arrival.
insights.implication: Support quietly with sponsored print runs, poster commissions and artist fees. Don't stage branded takeovers of these spaces.

hoops.headline: No streetball legends: here the game lives in school gyms, parishes and rec centers
hoops.summary: San Antonio has no WNBA team and no famous streetball cathedral. Its basketball runs on Spurs values, team-first, unflashy and international, and on neighborhood high schools, Catholic-school programs, rec centers and church leagues. After a 62-20 season and a Finals run, young hoopers grow up with Victor Wembanyama as the local hero. Go community-first: youth and school product, with bilingual, neighborhood-coded graphics.

insights.title: The Spurs are the whole basketball identity
insights.detail: There's no WNBA team and the college scene is modest, so nearly all local hoops pride runs through the Spurs. The Duncan-Parker-Ginobili era defined the city's idea of how the game should be played. The 2026 West title and Finals run have pushed that pride to a high.
insights.implication: Product tied to Spurs values (team ball, humility, craft) lands better than hype or star framing. Lead with the team and the shared city.

insights.title: Wembanyama is a generational local hero for kids
insights.detail: A 7-foot-4 French star, signed long-term, is the first role model for a generation of San Antonio kids. On courts around town, long-armed bigs with guard skills are now the aspiration.
insights.implication: Make youth sizes and kids' signature-line story a priority. Consider Wemby-adjacent youth product and clinics through licensed Spurs channels.

insights.title: Neighborhood and Catholic-school rivalries carry the grassroots
insights.detail: San Antonio prep basketball spans large public districts (Northside, North East, Judson, South San, Harlandale, Edgewood), plus TAPPS and private-school programs. Pride runs block by block and district by district, not citywide.
insights.implication: Team-sale and pack-out product coded to each school and district, in local school colors, will earn more trust than one citywide look.

insights.title: Tejano and Chicano style shows up on court
insights.detail: Many local hoopers are Mexican American. Fiesta color, papel picado, Tejano music and Spanish-language shorthand are part of how locals dress and brand teams and tournaments.
insights.implication: Use the community's language and color, with credit and local partners. Avoid generic south-of-the-border tropes.

insights.title: Military and bilingual family culture shape the youth game
insights.detail: Joint Base San Antonio families and a bicultural city make rec leagues, base gyms and church programs a real feeder. Many players move through the city for a few years.
insights.implication: Keep price points accessible and product durable and practice-ready. A military-appreciation tie-in could work through established programs.

insights.title: Pro-am and AAU play is rising but scattered
insights.detail: Summer leagues, AAU clubs and shoe-circuit travel teams are spread across the metro and nearby Austin. No single citywide pro-am brand dominates, as far as I can confirm.
insights.implication: Scout 2026 events before committing to a partner. Consider seeding product to a few respected local coaches and trainers.

fanbase.headline: One team, handed down: Spurs loyalty runs in families across South Texas
fanbase.summary: The only major-league team in town gets inherited loyalty, passed down in two languages from West Side abuelas to Joint Base San Antonio families and Austin-to-Laredo road-trippers. Duncan-era humility is still the house style, and Victor Wembanyama has added a young, French-speaking, global layer. Heading into 2026-27 the mood is confident and a little protective. Keep the product local and unshowy.

insights.title: One team, whole city, whole region
insights.detail: No other major-league franchise plays here, so the Spurs carry the identity of San Antonio, the Hill Country and the Rio Grande Valley. The Spurs Nation brand has long reached Laredo, Corpus Christi, Del Rio and across the border into Mexico.
insights.implication: Go regional and bilingual, not just downtown. Pop-ups and retail partnerships in South Texas and border-adjacent cities reach fans that a San Antonio-only plan misses.

insights.title: Understatement is the aesthetic
insights.detail: Fans take pride in a team that is the opposite of flashy. The Duncan-Popovich culture made silver, black and white with minimal graphics the default for 30 years, and the Spurs wordmark and spur logo read as heritage. Fans wear the Icon silver and black, the Fiesta-stripe City Edition and Duncan-era throwbacks.
insights.implication: Lead with clean silver-and-black execution, tonal logos and quality fabrics. Loud gradients and invented graphics feel off-brand here, unless they tie to Fiesta or a local story.

insights.title: Wembanyama made the base younger and global
insights.detail: Victor Wembanyama has brought a Gen Z, social-first, French-speaking crowd to Frost Bank Center. Kids wear his number 1 jersey, and tourists and international visitors are easy to spot among the Duncan-era diehards.
insights.implication: Build Wemby product in two lanes: a kids and youth range at accessible prices, and a premium collector lane. His signature line is the market's single biggest swing.

insights.title: The Finals loss left them hungry
insights.detail: A 62-win team beat OKC in seven to win the West, then lost the Finals to the Knicks 4-1. The core is locked up with Wembanyama and Fox extensions, and fans see a first chapter of a Wembanyama-Fox-Castle-Harper window, not a one-off. The Spurs are title co-favorites.
insights.implication: Look forward and keep it earned, building toward the 2027 playoffs. Don't commemorate a title that didn't happen, and avoid anything that reads as a premature celebration.

insights.title: The City Edition already speaks Fiesta
insights.detail: The Fiesta-stripe City Edition returns for 2026-27. It borrows the papel picado and colored cascarones palette of Fiesta San Antonio, which lands each April near the playoffs.
insights.implication: The City Edition is already the culture-first product, so build supporting capsules around it. April, with Fiesta and the playoffs together, is the strongest window.

insights.title: Military and Latino families are the backbone
insights.detail: San Antonio is Military City USA, home to Joint Base San Antonio. It is majority Latino, with strong Mexican American and Tejano traditions, and the Spurs have long held Military Appreciation and Hispanic Heritage nights.
insights.implication: Partner with local creators, and co-create the military and heritage nights instead of theming them. Credit and pay the Chicano and Tejano artists whose work informs the graphics.

rhythm.headline: Fiesta and the first playoff round share April, the city's loudest month
rhythm.summary: Engagement here is civic, and it peaks from April through June, when the playoffs overlap Fiesta and Cinco de Mayo. After the 2026 West title and the Finals loss to the Knicks, the baseline sits far above the rebuild years. The first product window runs from the Oct 20 opener against OKC to the Dec 25 rematch at the Knicks. In February the city turns to rodeo and western wear.

insights.title: Fiesta and the playoffs collide in April
insights.detail: Fiesta San Antonio runs about ten days in the second half of April and lands on the first playoff rounds. It brings Battle of Flowers, Fiesta Flambeau, NIOSA and the Fiesta medal culture. Medals, papel picado colors and cascarones are the local visual language of that fortnight.
insights.implication: Drop a Fiesta-stripe or Fiesta-palette playoff capsule in early April, not at the City Edition launch. Fans can wear it to watch parties and parades. Credit the local artists.

insights.title: February belongs to the Rodeo
insights.detail: The San Antonio Stock Show and Rodeo fills most of February around the Frost Bank Center, and the Spurs have long scheduled a multi-game Rodeo Road Trip away from home. Western wear (hats, boots, Wranglers) is the city's top retail category that month.
insights.implication: Fan engagement dips at home in February, but a Spurs-in-western-wear crossover is a one-month opportunity. Time a silver-and-black western shirt, trucker or belt buckle piece to rodeo opening.

insights.title: Silver and black is worn all year
insights.detail: Unlike in most markets, Spurs gear gets worn every month, including by military families at Fort Sam Houston, Lackland and Randolph, so baseline retail doesn't collapse in summer. Dips come from 100-degree heat and the Texas high-school football and Cowboys fall calendar, not from team indifference.
insights.implication: Keep core Association and Icon product in stock all year, and save limited drops for the peaks. A Military Appreciation tie-in is credible and local.

insights.title: 2026-27 is a title-chase season with a built-in Knicks story
insights.detail: The Spurs open at home Oct 20 against OKC, a West finals rematch on NBC and Peacock. They play the Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Christmas Day at noon ET, another Finals rematch, and host the Knicks Mar 7. Expectations are title co-favorite.
insights.implication: Christmas and Mar 7 are national-attention spikes for a Wembanyama-led product story. Hold the stars-and-hero graphics for those windows.

insights.title: Fall is the season of Muertos and the NBA Cup
insights.detail: Late October through early November pairs the season start with Dia de los Muertos in the West Side and Southtown (altars, ofrendas, calaveras). NBA Cup group play starts too, including Lakers at Spurs on Oct 30. The Fiesta-stripe City Edition uniform returns this season after its November 2025 debut.
insights.implication: Keep sacred Muertos imagery out of commerce unless community partners are involved. Use Fiesta color and papel picado craft cues instead, and credit local artists.

insights.title: Project Marvel shapes sentiment
insights.detail: The planned downtown arena is a roughly $1.3B project within a larger district, and it is at least five years out. The team ran a summer 2026 community listening tour and is seeking lease amendments at the Frost Bank Center. Fans are proud of the team but sensitive about public money and neighborhoods.
insights.implication: Skip downtown-arena and Frost Bank Center nostalgia product until the story settles. Frame it around the East Side and West Side communities, not the skyline.

uniform.headline: The Fiesta stripe is back, and the next local story is still up for grabs
uniform.summary: The official palette is deliberately austere: black, silver and white, the look of the Duncan-Popovich dynasty and now of Wembanyama. Fans' warmest memory is the Fiesta era, the teal, orange and fuchsia of the late 1980s to 2002. The Fiesta-stripe City Edition returns in 2026-27 on a Finals-run high. Which local story comes next is still open.

insights.title: Silver and black is the identity, Fiesta the love
insights.detail: The core palette is near-monochrome and signals discipline, the Duncan-era brand. Fans' warmest nostalgia belongs to the multi-color Fiesta era, and a Fiesta-stripe City Edition brought it back.
insights.implication: Use Fiesta color as an accent layer on silver-and-black bases, not a replacement. Stripes, trims and tonal prints beat full-color takeovers.

insights.title: The Fiesta-stripe City Edition returns for 2026-27
insights.detail: Unveiled in November 2025 and repeating this season, it pairs a black base with Fiesta-colored chest and shorts stripes. A repeat City Edition after a Finals run has a built-in sell-through window.
insights.implication: Build the 2026-27 merch story around the returning jersey: warm-up, tees, shorts and kids product keyed to the stripe. Time the drops to Fiesta in April.

insights.title: Los Spurs and Noche Latina are the community-proven lane
insights.detail: The team has long run Noche Latina and Los Spurs branding for Latino heritage nights. The Spanish-language identity predates the Nike era and suits a majority Mexican-American city.
insights.implication: Co-create heritage-night product with San Antonio designers, and write the copy in Spanish first. Don't translate a template made in Portland.

insights.title: Wembanyama gives silver and black a global second audience
insights.detail: Wembanyama's French and international following, plus games scheduled in Paris and Manchester, make the classic palette travel. The Spurs also sit near the Mexican border, with a large fanbase in Monterrey and northern Mexico.
insights.implication: Pair a clean Icon and Association story for global buyers with a Spanish-language South Texas and Mexico story for regional product.

insights.title: Military San Antonio is a recurring uniform platform
insights.detail: Military Appreciation nights are a fixture in a city with Joint Base San Antonio and a deep veteran community. Military looks have been a Spurs staple, tied to the Popovich-era ethos.
insights.implication: Go camo-free and tonal, in silver and black with subtle texture, in partnership with veteran groups. Don't commercialize service insignia.

insights.title: Local bootleg and print culture sets the street standard
insights.detail: San Antonio shirt culture favors Spurs-adjacent graphics from local shops and screen printers: the 210 area code, Alamo City, the Spurs skyline and Tejano-leaning typography. Fans reward the real thing and punish corporate gloss.
insights.implication: Collaborate with named local brands on limited drops. Don't compete with their visual language.

retail-landscape.headline: Spurs gear sells at the mall, but the West Side decides what's cool
retail-landscape.summary: After the Finals run, Spurs demand crosses generations and flows through volume doors: mall chains, Academy, Dick's and the arena team store. Taste comes from Chicano and Tejano style, Fiesta and military-family practicality. The Fiesta-stripe City Edition shows local color sells. Pair the big doors with credible community pop-ups, not a flagship this mall-and-Academy city may not need.

insights.title: Volume lives in malls and Academy
insights.detail: San Antonio shops for gear at North Star Mall, La Cantera, Rolling Oaks, Ingram Park and South Park Mall chains, plus Academy Sports + Outdoors and Dillard's. There is no single downtown flagship.
insights.implication: Win with allocation and shop-in-shop quality at Foot Locker, Champs, Academy and Dick's before investing in a destination door.

insights.title: The arena store is a ritual door
insights.detail: Families drive in from across South Texas on game nights, and the Frost Bank Center team store is where Spurs-specific and City Edition items launch.
insights.implication: Use it for City Edition drops, player-night exclusives and Wemby/Fox/Castle/Harper collections. Plan around Project Marvel's long-term downtown move.

insights.title: West Side and Southtown set taste
insights.detail: Credibility comes from West Side Chicano and Tejano style, the Southtown and Blue Star creative scenes, and Market Square. The north-side malls don't set it.
insights.implication: Seed product through community pop-ups and local creators in those neighborhoods, credited and paid, before it hits mass doors.

insights.title: Fiesta is the retail season
insights.detail: April's Fiesta is a San Antonio-only apparel and accessories moment, with medals, flower-crown colors and papel picado. It overlaps playoff time.
insights.implication: Time Fiesta-color capsules and Spurs playoff product together. The Fiesta-stripe City Edition gives you the story.

insights.title: Military and South Texas reach widen the base
insights.detail: Joint Base San Antonio families and fans from the Rio Grande Valley, Laredo and Mexico shop on trips to San Antonio. Many buy at outlets and malls along the I-35 corridor.
insights.implication: Stock size runs and value tiers for family and military shoppers. Test Spanish-language and cross-border marketing around the outlet corridor.

insights.title: Sneaker credibility is thin and local
insights.detail: San Antonio's independent sneaker scene is smaller than Houston's or Dallas's. Credibility spreads across resellers, consignment and pop-up events, with no anchor boutique.
insights.implication: Partner with local resellers and event promoters for basketball launches. Verify which independents are active before committing.

retail-behavior.headline: Paydays, families and the Fiesta calendar set the shopping clock
retail-behavior.summary: This is a big, price-aware, majority-Latino market with a large military and healthcare workforce, and most people already own some Spurs gear. After the 2026 West title and Finals run, demand is at a franchise high. Tier the product so a family of four, a Fort Sam Houston E-5 and an Alamo Heights collector each find a way in.

insights.title: The August tax-free weekend is the real back-to-school start
insights.detail: Texas runs an annual sales-tax holiday on a weekend in early-to-mid August (Friday to Sunday; 2027 dates to confirm). Clothing, footwear and school supplies under $100 per item skip the normal 8.25% San Antonio combined rate. Spurs fans, many shopping for several kids at once, plan around it and pull forward sneakers, tees and shorts.
insights.implication: Hold a sub-$100 hero tier so the product lands under the threshold: kids' and youth sizes, tees, shorts, slides, and Spurs graphic hoodies on promo. Authentic jerseys sit above it and won't benefit.

insights.title: Fiesta is the local Super Bowl for apparel, and Spurs gear lives inside it
insights.detail: Fiesta San Antonio in April is a ten-day citywide celebration. It brings parades (Battle of Flowers, Fiesta Flambeau), Fiesta Medal culture and Night in Old San Antonio at La Villita. Locals buy and trade commemorative medals and wear Fiesta colors. It often overlaps the playoff push.
insights.implication: Drop a Fiesta colorway in early April, with medal-pin or patch accessories. The City Edition's Fiesta stripes are the bridge. Fans already shop for this ritual, so join it.

insights.title: Military paydays and the base exchange shape the calendar and the price ceiling
insights.detail: Joint Base San Antonio (Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, Randolph) puts a large population on a 1st-and-15th pay cycle. Deployment send-offs and homecomings drive gifting. Many service members and families shop on-base exchanges and online, not at mall flagships.
insights.implication: Plan launches and promo codes around the 1st and 15th. Consider a military-appreciation capsule or first-responder pricing. Build it with the Spurs' existing military-night programming, not Nike alone.

insights.title: Heat sets the product mix, and the hoodie window is short but sharp
insights.detail: Summers regularly run into the upper 90s and 100s, and the playoff run falls in the hottest months. Cold fronts (northers) arrive abruptly between December and February. Each one sparks a sudden run on hoodies, fleece and warm-ups for a few days.
insights.implication: Lead year-round with breathable tees, shooting shirts, shorts and lightweight tops. Keep fleece and warm-ups to smaller, fast-replenishment buys, timed to the first cold snaps and the Christmas gifting run.

insights.title: Mexico and South Texas fans shop San Antonio as a regional hub
insights.detail: Shoppers from Laredo, the Rio Grande Valley and northern Mexico (Monterrey and Nuevo Laredo especially) drive to San Antonio for malls and outlets. The big draws are La Cantera, North Star and the San Marcos Premium Outlets. Trips cluster around Mexico's Buen Fin in November and the December holidays. Spurs fandom in Mexico is long-established, through the team's Mexican-market presence and the NBA's Mexico City games.
insights.implication: Make Spanish-language and bilingual messaging standard on drops. Align promos with Buen Fin and December travel weekends. Confirm inventory in border-region stores rather than assuming the demand is only Bexar County's.

insights.title: Jersey buying is tiered by income, and Wembanyama has reset the stack
insights.detail: Fans buy up and down a wide ladder. It runs from swingman and kids' replica jerseys to tees with a player name and number. At the bottom are knockoff and bootleg designs at flea markets such as Traders Village and Mission Marketplace. Since the Finals run, demand centers on Wembanyama, with Fox, Castle and Harper the other name-and-number buys.
insights.implication: Keep a clear good-better-best ladder of tee, swingman and authentic. Protect launch moments for the authentic tier with limited drops. Don't chase flea-market price points with the top tier.

insights.title: Holiday and heritage moments matter more than a generic retail calendar
insights.detail: Gifting here follows Christmas and Las Posadas, Dia de los Muertos (late October to November 2), Mother's Day, Easter and quinceanera season. The San Antonio Stock Show and Rodeo in February adds a dress-up and Western-wear moment. Many of these are family purchases, not self-purchases.
insights.implication: Build gift-ready sets and family bundles around Christmas and Mother's Day. Treat Dia de los Muertos and rodeo season as design inspiration, but only through local creator partnerships.

extra.priceProfile: San Antonio is price-aware. Median household income sits below the national and Texas averages, with a wide spread by neighborhood. The West and South Sides and military households are value-minded. Alamo Heights, Stone Oak and the Hill Country are affluent. Texas has no state income tax but an 8.25% combined sales tax, so the August holiday and promos matter. Tier it clearly: a sub-$100 entry, a mid-range swingman and premium tees, and a limited authentic top.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Tees and kids' replica jerseys are the volume. Swingmen are the committed-fan buy. Authentics come mainly from collectors and higher-income households. Name-and-number demand centers on Wembanyama, with Fox, Castle and Harper behind. Throwback Duncan, Ginobili and Parker items work with older fans. The City Edition is a major seasonal purchase, especially as it returns with the Fiesta stripes for 2026-27.

factcheck.summary: The dossiers largely match the verified current facts (record, Finals loss, extensions, City Edition, dates), so few outright errors turned up. Fixed: the Alamodome "first home" error, the Farfisa and Sunglows details, the Southwest School of Art's move to UTSA and the Tobin Center symphony line. Also fixed: a Texas rodeo naming slip, an MLK Day entry implying a Spurs game, inflated "largest Mexican market" claims and two off-palette red hex values. Live checks confirmed the San Marcos Nike Factory Store and Hogwild Records, and corrected the art school. The strategy brief needs an editor on three points. One is the claim that no hand-made West Side vocabulary has reached a Spurs uniform. Another is the Feb 15 Spurs-Heat "road game" premise. The third is unverified player footwear deals. Most local businesses and artists are long-established but unchecked today.

issues.problem: Rotulo only half passes the swap test. Sign-painter lettering, talavera tile and lowrider pinstripe are shared Mexican-American and border imagery, found in Los Angeles, Houston, El Paso and across Mexico. Talavera is Pueblan. The brief's own dossiers show the San Antonio-only material is conjunto, Fiesta medals and the West Side shop-sign scene. "Reads as nobody but San Antonio" is overclaimed, and a cream base with cobalt and candy red could be a Houston or Santa Fe jersey.
issues.fix: Anchor the concept in San Antonio-only specifics. Draw the letterforms from named West Side shop signs, by a commissioned local sign painter. Use the conjunto accordion as the structural pattern and Fiesta-medal ribbon colors as the palette. Drop talavera and the generic pinstripe unless a named San Antonio maker supplies them. Cut the "nobody but" claim.

issues.problem: The sequencing doesn't work. The Fiesta-stripe City Edition covers 2025-26 and 2026-27, so the next new San Antonio City Edition is 2027-28. Nike and NBA concept lock for that cycle normally falls 12-18 months before the November 2027 reveal, which means mid-to-late 2026. A ground-up hand-lettered pitch now risks missing the window. The NBA and Spurs must also approve jersey numeral legibility, wordmark treatment, court changes and a live-painted baseline wordmark.
issues.fix: Pitch Rotulo now, and ask Nike Basketball Apparel and the NBA for the real lock date first. Use the Rotulo pieces that need no uniform approval (warm-up, shooting shirt, cap, tee) as the near-term proof of concept. Keep the court painting as an option.

issues.problem: A jock tag reading "Hecho a mano en San Antonio" on a factory-made jersey is a labeling and trust risk. The lettering is hand-drawn, but the garment is neither hand-made nor made in San Antonio, and a city that prizes real craft will notice. NBA jock-tag layout is also standardized.
issues.fix: Credit the artist as designer, for example "Lettering by [name], San Antonio". Save "hecho a mano" for the hand-pulled screenprint tees. Check tag placement with the NBA.

issues.problem: The brief routes Misiones through the National Park Service and the parishes. But the missions sit on Coahuiltecan and other Indigenous ground and were built with Indigenous labor, and no Indigenous voice appears among the brief's partners. The mission rose window and arches are also live sacred architecture. The Plata y Negro "mission-arch jacquard" has the same problem in softer form.
issues.fix: Add a named Indigenous consultation step, with credit and pay, before any mission geometry reaches product. Start with the Tap Pilam Coahuiltecan Nation or comparable local Native organizations. Otherwise drop the mission geometry from core product and keep the alternate on the shelf.

issues.problem: The brief calls Hemisfair and the Tower of the Americas the safest skyline mark. But Hemisfair is also the downtown redevelopment area. The Project Marvel downtown district sits in the same civic conversation, with the public-money sensitivities the brief itself flags as a risk. The brief says to keep skyline nostalgia off product, yet it keeps this as an alternate.
issues.fix: Verify the Project Marvel site and the Tower of the Americas licensing before going further. If the district is adjacent, use the 1968 fair's typography only and avoid the skyline.

issues.problem: Black San Antonio and the East Side are missing from the whole brief. The arena it is built around sits on the East Side. George Gervin is the franchise's first star, and the Iceman finger-roll era is the root of the Spurs' fan lineage. Duncan, Elliott and Johnson-era Black fans are part of the one-team city. Project Marvel moving the team off the East Side is the neighborhood story most likely to matter there. The brief's partners, artists and cues are almost all Chicano and Tejano.
issues.fix: Add an East Side thread. Put a Gervin-era look in a Classic Edition capsule and credit a Black San Antonio designer or illustrator. Start a partnership talk with East Side institutions such as the Carver Community Cultural Center (verify status). Rewrite the thesis from "majority-Latino" to the whole city.

issues.problem: Tejano Conjunto Festival celebrates traditional conjunto, and the brief's only musical partner is a punk band that brings accordion to a younger crowd. That misses the people the festival belongs to: Guadalupe-linked conjunto players and families, and the legacy of Flaco Jimenez (died in 2025, verify), the city's most beloved accordionist. A festival-week drop without elders or the estate reads as borrowing. Any Flaco likeness also needs estate licensing.
issues.fix: Lead with the Guadalupe Cultural Arts Center and a conjunto musician or ensemble named on the product. Keep Pinata Protest as the younger-scene complement. Treat a Flaco tribute as a licensing talk with his family, never an image on a tee.

issues.problem: The Dec 25 game tips at noon ET, 11 a.m. in San Antonio on Christmas morning. Ice-house watch-party kits tied to it are unrealistic, because ice houses and families are at home. Gift product must be in hand by mid-December, not pushed on the day. The brief also misses that Cup quarterfinals on Dec 4-5 and semifinals on Dec 8-9 are now played at the higher seed's home arena. The Spurs are in West Group C. They could host a knockout game in the exact window the brief spends on gifting.
issues.fix: Move watch-party launches to Cup Fridays, Thanksgiving week and Mar 7. Keep Dec 25 for a digital and gifting moment. Add a conditional plan for a Cup knockout home game (Dec 4-9), with the stripe family ready.

issues.problem: The opening-night relaunch assumes the City Edition is on shelf and in use by Oct 20 and Oct 30. Last season it was unveiled in November, and the first-wear date for a repeat City Edition is unconfirmed. Product for Oct 20 is already built, so the real lever in the next 11 days is allocation, not new design.
issues.fix: Verify the 2026-27 City Edition first-wear date. If it is November, make Oct 20 an Association and Icon moment with stripe teaser content, and move the stripe push to the first City Edition game.

issues.target: opportunities[fiesta-playoff-drop] / collection numbered playoff medal set
issues.problem: A numbered medal per playoff round depends on an outcome nobody controls. If the Spurs lose in round one, most of the set never ships. A one-per-round clock also invites sell-through risk and collector resentment. The regular season ends Apr 11 and the playoffs start about a week later, so the drop lands before Fiesta and before round one is set. Fiesta medals also belong to hundreds of local organizations, military units, schools and neighborhoods. A Nike-made medal could look like it is crowding out the small makers who make the real ones.
issues.fix: Release the medal set as one pre-announced bundle (for example, four pieces) at the April drop, not round by round. Commission local medal makers or Fiesta organizations to produce it, and share proceeds. Lock the Fiesta Commission rights and artist contracts by December.

issues.problem: The brief puts the "first week of April" drop ahead of Fiesta, but Fiesta's 2027 dates are unverified and may land after the first playoff games. Fiesta events (Battle of Flowers, Flambeau, NIOSA) are also community-run and not mainly a shopping window. The arena is not where Fiesta fans are that week.
issues.fix: Confirm the 2027 Fiesta dates and check them against the Apr 11 end of season. Make the drop wearable at Fiesta events (pin-ready caps, lightweight shirts). Sell through Market Square and community partners, not the arena.

issues.problem: The calendar opens in the past. The August tax holiday has passed, and Hispanic Heritage Month (Sep 15 to Oct 15) is already under way, so a September "preview" can't happen. The Wembanyama youth ladder is rated priority 1, but its next anchor moment is August 2027, ten months out. Beyond "refresh", it says nothing about the October-December youth plan.
issues.fix: Start the live calendar at Oct 9 with the remaining Heritage Month days, Oct 20, Oct 30 and Nov. Make the youth ladder an always-on tier: a holiday and Christmas push now, with August as the peak.

issues.problem: Pearl snaps, western yokes and rope caps are Texas-wide and could belong to Houston (where the Rodeo is bigger) or Fort Worth. The product list undercuts the brief's own rule against cowboy cliches. The San Antonio-specific part, the Stock Show and Rodeo at the Freeman grounds and the Spurs Rodeo Road Trip, is under-used.
issues.fix: Build the capsule around the Rodeo Road Trip itself: a road-trip stripe, trip-city patches, and a commissioned San Antonio Western-wear maker or Mexican-American vaquero tradition (charro heritage), credited by name. Otherwise cut it.

issues.problem: San Japan is a good local signal, but the brief ties a Wembanyama collectible graphic to anime and gaming IP. Licensing third-party IP and fitting Wembanyama's personal brand both need his team and Nike to approve. The idea is priority 3, with months 1 and 8 spanning unrelated events, and it isn't grounded in the San Antonio insights.
issues.fix: Cut it to a single test pop-up at San Japan, with original Wembanyama-approved art and no third-party IP. Or drop it and fold the Paris and Manchester travel set into the Nike app.

issues.problem: The brief says the fan base runs to Monterrey and northern Mexico, but offers no Mexico-side plan beyond Buen Fin promotions at Texas malls. It also treats the in-state Austin game as a date to verify, not a market. Austin is split among Spurs, Rockets and Mavs fans, and I-35 makes it a Spurs pop-up opportunity. Mexico shoppers also arrive on cross-border weekends that don't map neatly to Buen Fin.
issues.fix: Add an Austin game-week pop-up plan. Once verified, name the border-region partners (Laredo and Rio Grande Valley retailers, the Spurs' existing Mexico programming). Check cross-border shopping weeks and the Mexican peso before setting allocations.

issues.problem: The military capsule has no named partner. "A veteran-owned local partner" and "the Spurs' program" are placeholders, and Joint Base San Antonio exchange sales (AAFES) need their own approval path, which the brief marks "if approved". David Robinson's Navy lineage is a strong, specific hook, but the brief never turns it into a product story.
issues.fix: Name a specific partner, such as a veteran-owned local brand or an established veterans nonprofit. Use Robinson's story (Naval Academy, the Admiral) as a tonal graphic idea. Treat exchange distribution as a stretch and leave it out of the KPI.

issues.problem: Cruz Ortiz, Alex Rubio, Adriana Garcia and Pinata Protest are real and credible, but the brief assumes their availability and Nike's standard terms. Murals carry rights and property questions, and "revenue share" conflicts with how Nike normally commissions artists. Four artists is also thin for a market the brief calls hand-made at every level, and none are women printmakers or younger makers.
issues.fix: Verify availability, then add a few younger and women artists through the Guadalupe Cultural Arts Center's open call. Set paid commission terms and a royalty structure with Nike legal before any outreach.

issues.problem: The risk list misses the biggest local sentiment risk. The Finals loss to the Knicks makes the Dec 25 and Mar 7 product a sore spot, and the brief says only "avoid commemorating". It also skips counterfeit and bootleg pressure on a returning, popular City Edition. Last, it ignores the licensing complexity of the Wembanyama, Fox, Castle and Harper footwear affiliations for any player-led campaign.
issues.fix: Add explicit rules: no Knicks-baiting graphics and no title or Finals language. Check the player's footwear affiliation on every named-player style before it enters the plan.

strengths: The central insight is unmistakably San Antonio: silver and black as civic dress, with Fiesta as the occasion. Fans' real reaction to the Fiesta-stripe City Edition backs it up.
The rules against a full-color Fiesta takeover, and against the Alamo, mission interiors, Dia de los Muertos, sombreros and Selena, are specific and mostly right.

The tiering logic is grounded in retail behavior: a sub-$100 youth ladder at Academy and Dick's, a protected top tier, and a bootleg price floor at Traders Village. The volume-versus-taste split is honest about a thin independent sneaker scene.
Commissioning, naming and paying West Side artists on the neck label, with proceeds to the Guadalupe Cultural Arts Center, is the right way to be credible.
The 2026-27 tone is forward-looking ("unfinished"). That matches fan sentiment after the Finals loss and avoids premature title product.
The calendar anchors are well chosen, and only San Antonio has them. They are Contemporary Art Month, the Mar 5 First Friday two days before the Mar 7 Knicks game, Fiesta and the Rodeo Road Trip.
critique.summary: A strong, locally literate brief. Its Fiesta-and-restraint thesis, tiered retail logic and paid-artist model could only be San Antonio. The weak points: Rotulo overclaims and leans on border-wide visual language, and its City Edition lock date needs checking. The medal set depends on playoff outcomes, and some calendar items are already past or unrealistic on Christmas morning. The brief also sees only Latino San Antonio. Black San Antonio and the East Side (Gervin, the arena's neighborhood) are missing, and so are Indigenous voices on the missions. Fix the sequencing and add those voices before anything is pitched.
